title: Google Unveils Gemini Intelligent Eyewear From $395, On Sale December 10
excerpt: The display-free Android XR glasses, made with Samsung, Warby Parker and Gentle Monster, pair Gemini voice help with a 12-megapixel camera - but only with Pixel, select Galaxy and newer iPhones at launch.
body:
• Google opened pre-orders on November 12 for Intelligent Eyewear, its Gemini-powered audio glasses made with Samsung, Warby Parker and Gentle Monster, with sales starting December 10.
  • Prices start at $395 for Warby Parker's three styles and $449 for Gentle Monster's six styles; the frames have no display and weigh around 41 grams.
  • Compatibility is narrow at launch: Pixel 7 and newer, select Samsung Galaxy phones on One UI 9 or later, and iPhone 13 Pro and later - other Android brands are not supported yet.
  • Reader utility: check your phone model before pre-ordering; battery is rated up to nine hours, and the 12-megapixel camera records photos and video with an indicator light that cannot be covered without stopping recording.

Google has opened pre-orders for Intelligent Eyewear, its first Android XR smart glasses, built around the Gemini assistant and made in collaboration with Samsung, Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Google announced the collections on November 12 in its official announcement, with availability in stores and online on December 10.

What the glasses do

The first generation has no display in the lenses. Gemini help arrives by voice, through open-ear speakers, using a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera, microphones and a touch surface on the frame. Saying "Hey Gemini" or tapping the frame lets wearers ask questions about what they are looking at, get turn-by-turn Google Maps directions in the ear, and receive real-time Google Translate speech translation with automatic language detection across more than 70 languages, according to Google.

Google also lists multi-step tasks handled in the background, such as adding an item in view to a grocery list, checking Calendar availability from an event poster, replying to messages, taking calls hands-free, and playing music or audiobooks from YouTube Music, Spotify, Apple Music and Audible. A feature called Guided Vision offers conversational audio descriptions for people who are blind or have low vision, and a link with Aira lets users stream the camera feed to a trained human visual interpreter.

Hardware, price and availability

The frames weigh around 41 grams and are rated for up to nine hours of battery life, with a charging case that can recharge them up to seven times, Google says. Android Police reports the glasses run Qualcomm's Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 chipset and that the camera supports HDR processing and image stabilisation. Warby Parker's collection - Alden, Reid and Wren - starts at $395 in the United States and Canada, in optical or sun styles. Gentle Monster's six designs start at $449 and launch in the United States and South Korea. Both collections go on sale December 10, according to Android Police and Google.

Compatibility limits

Compatibility is the main caveat. At launch the glasses work only with Google Pixel 7 and newer models, select Samsung Galaxy smartphones running One UI 9 or later, and iPhone 13 Pro and later. Other Android brands, including Honor, Xiaomi and Oppo phones, are not supported, Android Police reports. Google's own announcement describes the glasses more broadly as working with Pixel and Samsung phones as well as iPhones, without listing every model, so buyers should confirm their exact phone against the launch list before paying.

Privacy design

Google says camera visuals used for Gemini questions are not saved in Gemini History and are not used to train AI models or target ads, and that bystanders' faces are automatically redacted from those visuals before Gemini processes them. An indicator light shows when a photo or video is being captured for the gallery, and the glasses are designed to stop recording if the light is covered or disabled. Every pair also has an off switch so the frames can be worn as regular glasses. Those are Google's stated protections; how they hold up in everyday use will be tested after the December 10 launch.
